children: President Trump said Friday that Russia agreed to supply diesel to U.S. and global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices ahead of ‌the U.S. midterm elections, although analysts said the import amounts likely would be too small to significantly impact U.S. supplies.

Trump said on social media that Russia's Vladimir Putin agreed to "immediately" supply more than 300K tons of diesel fuel into the U.S. and global markets, another 500K tons in November, followed by another 1M tons, adding that Russia would later deliver an additional 3M tons of diesel "within a short period of time," based on the condition of its refineries.
Russia measures diesel quantities in tons, so the initial 300K tons to be delivered would equal ​2.25M barrels; by comparison, the U.S. exports 1.5M bbl/day of diesel.
After the first shipment, the 500K-ton release would equal 3.7M barrels, or 123K bbl/day, or less than 10% of U.S. daily exports.
The U.S. Treasury Department issued a waiver allowing importation of previously sanctioned Russian diesel until April 7.

Nymex diesel futures extended earlier losses and were down 4% post-market at $4.6828/gal on the news, although there was little reaction in crude oil futures, which inched lower after settling slightly higher Friday.

"The barrels could help, but they may not fully materialize, and what does arrive could still be too little, too late," CIBC Private Wealth Group senior energy trader Rebecca Babin said. "The headline may move prices initially, but this is hardly a straightforward solution."

"I cannot overstate how much of a nothing burger this is," as the amount of diesel to be delivered - if it is delivered at all - is not enough to lead to sustained lower prices, Rory Johnston, an oil market researcher and founder of CommodityContext.com, ​said on X.

"It's unclear to me how much additional supplies the world is actually going to get," due to the poor state of Russia's refineries after Ukrainian strikes and its own export restrictions, Lipow Oil Associates president Andy Lipow told
The Wall Street Journal
Russia suspended diesel exports earlier this year following Ukraine's strikes against Russian refineries, and last month the government extended its suspension of diesel exports until October 31.

"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy," Ukraine's President Zelenskyy said in reaction to Trump's move.

U.S. retail diesel prices stood at ~$6.28/gal on Friday, according to the American Automobile Association, after reaching a record $6.52/gal on September 22, but have not fallen substantially since Trump signed an executive order this week aiming to increase the availability of red-dyed diesel.

Crude oil futures edged higher Friday, as Trump's comments that the U.S. would not strike Iran before the midterm elections were balanced by concerns about continued attacks on shipping in the Middle East and the potential loss of U.S. production to Hurricane Isaias.
Front-month Nymex crude
for November delivery and front-month Brent crude
for December delivery both gained 0.4% on Friday to settle at $91.85/bbl and $104.72/bbl, respectively; for the full week, Nymex and Brent crude rose 0.8% and 2.4%.
Front-month Nymex ULSD (
) for November delivery fell 2.9% on Friday to $4.7384/gal, and front-month Nymex RBOB November gasoline (
) slipped 0.6% to $3.2952/gal; for the week, ULSD jumped 5.3% but RBOB lost 0.5%.
U.S. natural gas futures
recouped the previous day's losses on Friday, with the front-month November contract rising 1.6% to end the week up 6.1% at $3.22/MMBtu.
Energy stocks, as represented by the State Street Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF
, rose 3.6% this week.

title: Trump turns to Russia in bid to lower diesel prices, but analysts see minimal impact
